title: Structure and evolution of shark ribosomal DNA internal transcribed spacers

abstract_text: Internal transcribed spacers (ITS1 and ITS2) are DNA regions separating the multicopy, nuclear ribosomal RNA genes. We have obtained complete ITS2 sequences from several sharks representing different lineages, and report here on aspects of the comparative structure and evolution of this locus. Shark ITS2 regions are the largest reported for any eukaryote, a size explained in part by the insertion of sequence elements strongly resembling group I introns. These insertion elements appear to be present in all major shark lineages. They are, however, conspicuously absent from hammerhead sharks, arguing for an ancient origin of these elements with subsequent loss in the presumably derived hammerhead lineage. The insertion element is also absent from the ITS2 of the one stingray (Urolophus jamaicensis) we have examined thus far. We have also explored the phylogenetic utility of ITS2 sequences for resolving some relationships within the family Carcharhinidae. The precise affinities of Prionace and Negaprion to Carcharhinus are currently unsettled, with hypotheses proposed about Prionace being either a derived species within or sister taxon to Carcharhinus. Preliminary phylogenetic analysis of ITS2 sequences places Prionace well within the Carcharhinus clade, arguing against the current status of the blue shark as a separate genus.

abstract_text: Blue sharks are highly vagile elasmobranchs with a circumglobal temperate and tropical distribution. This species displays complex reproductive and migratory behavior, making it difficult to realize a clear picture of genetic stock structure. We report here our examination of the utility of mitochondrial (mt) DNA control region sequences for assessing blue shark genetic structure on a global scale. Complete control region (1069 bp in size) sequences were obtained from 16 blue shark individuals collected from 5 globally distributed sites. Contrary to the case in most vertebrates, this locus is remarkably conserved in blue sharks. The 11 haplotypes observed differed from each other by 5 or less single nucleotide substitutions or indels over the entire control region. Most of the genetic variation (8 of 12 variable sites) was restricted to the 350 bp region adjacent to the tRNA-proline gene, with no variation observed in the central 400 bp section of this locus. Phylogenetic analysis revealed no indication of geographic population structuring. We infer from these data that either the blue shark mt control region may be too conserved to be useful for population genetic studies, or that dispersal over a global scale is occurring, or has occurred in the recent past.

abstract_text: The basic structure of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) includes at least nine different forms found across the vertebrates. Some forms are believed to serve extrapituitary functions, as indicated by their wide distribution throughout the brain. Chicken II GnRH (cII) is considered the most evolutionarily conserved variant because it is generally found to coexist with at least one other form in all the jawed vertebrate classes, while dogfish GnRH (df) is found exclusively in elasmobranch fishes. This study examined the distribution of df and cII GnRH-immunoreactive (ir) cell bodies and fibers in the brain of the Atlantic stingray, Dasyatis sabina, by immunocytochemical methods as a first step to correlate anatomical distribution with possible functionality of the different forms in an elasmobranch. Dogfish GnRH-ir cells and fibers were localized in the ganglia of the terminal nerve and throughout the ventro-caudal telencephalon and preoptic area, while a large, discrete cII GnRH-ir cell nucleus was found in the midbrain tegmentum with main projections to the diencephalon and hindbrain. This is the first study to show differential distribution of cII and df GnRH in the elasmobranch brain, and supports the hypothesis of divergent function of GnRH variants such as gonadotropin control and neuromodulation of sensory function.

abstract_text: In the absence of bone marrow and lymph nodes, elasmobranch fish must rely on alternative lymphomyeloid tissues for production of immune cells. Principle tissues include spleen, thymus, epigonal organ, and, in some species, Leydig organ. To investigate the role of spleen in immune cell production, spleens were removed surgically from juvenile nurse sharks, Ginglymostoma cirratum, (n=8). Sham operated (n=5) and non-operated (n=5) juveniles served as controls. Peripheral blood, from which hematocrits and differential white cell counts were obtained, was sampled at varying intervals during the first week after surgery, then at weekly intervals for five weeks. Animals were sacrificed at various times for histological examination of lymphomyeloid tissues. Hematocrits did not vary significantly during the study. Circulating levels of lymphocytes decreased during the first three days, after which levels gradually returned to normal ranges within two to three weeks. Granulocyte levels increased initially and recovered after approximately three weeks. Preliminary assessment of tissue imprints indicates an increase in immature lymphocytes and granulocytes in epigonal organs of splenectomized animals compared with controls, suggesting that epigonal organ may increase its production of lymphocytes in the absence of spleen, but not at the expense of its role in granulocyte production.

title: Hormonal regulation of growth in vertebral cartilage of the clearnose skate, Raja eglanteria

abstract_text: In most elasmobranchs, growth of vertebral cartilage proceeds incrementally and forms periodic marks that are extensively used in age and growth studies. Such research is essential for the management of these fishes, yet is often limited by poor understanding of the physiological processes that regulate vertebral growth. Since skeletal growth in most vertebrates is under strict control of the endocrine system, the goal of this study was to investigate the hormonal regulation of vertebral growth in the clearnose skate, Raja eglanteria. Synthesis of cartilage matrix glycosaminoglycans (GAG) was used as a marker for vertebral growth using an in vitro culture system. The effects of growth hormone (GH), insulin-like growth factor-I (IGF-I), tri-iodo-L-thyronine (T3), and corticosteroids on GAG synthesis were assessed, due to their well-documented roles in cartilage growth. The effect of calcitonin (CT) on vertebral growth was also investigated, due to its involvement in the skeletal physiology and mineral homeostasis of terrestrial vertebrates. Finally, the effect of parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrp) on GAG synthesis was examined, because of its critical role in mammalian skeletogenesis. PTHrp has recently been detected in the perichondrium of elasmobranch vertebral cartilage, thus it may play a role in chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation. The present study is the first investigation on the hormonal regulation of elasmobranch skeletal physiology.

title: Mechanics of ventilation in the swellshark, Cephaloscyllium ventriosum (Scyliorhinidae)

authors.affiliation: University of California, Irvine, CA 92697-2525 USA

abstract_text: Most fishes are faced with one of two options for gill ventilation: physically moving their gills through the medium ("ram" ventilation), or actively pumping the medium over their gills via "buccal pumping". The basic pattern of mechanical movements during buccal pumping was studied over 40 years ago. However, unique patterns of water flow through the head of the swellshark during feeding suggested that the generation of respiratory currents might not be as simple as once thought. Using pressure transducers implanted into the buccal and gill cavities of actively respiring swellsharks, it was discovered that pressure traces vary within and among individuals. These data, combined with both video and electrical impedance data for the displacement of the lower jaw and gill septum, suggest that although the classic pattern of pressure generation regularly occurs, at least one novel pattern of pressure generation exists. During this novel pattern, pressure reversals exist over a much longer duration than previously thought possible, and at much larger magnitudes. It is questionable whether the classic alternating "suction" and "pressure" pumps are always used for moving water over the gills unidirectionally, and whether continuous water flow over the gills exists for large intervals of time in this species.

title: Ontogenetic changes in energetics and active and passive ventilation of the swell shark (Cephaloscyllium ventriosum) egg capsule

abstract_text: The swell shark, Cephaloscyllium ventriosum, is an oviparous chondrichthyan fish. Each egg capsule contains a single embryo that is incubated on the sea floor for 7.5 to 10 months. The horny capsule material is not sufficiently permeable to oxygen to supply the needs of a late stage embryo, however, after about one third of development four slits open in the sides of the egg case to admit seawater. We investigated ontogenetic changes in metabolic rate and mechanisms of capsule ventilation. Mass specific rate of oxygen consumption decreases as the embryo grows. Early stage embryos have a relatively large tail appendage that is used to generate a water current through the capsule. During development this appendage decreases in relative size and just before hatching the embryo ventilates the capsule by oropharyngeal pumping. In addition to the active pumping, the capsule is ventilated passively. When in a current, pressure differences along the capsule induce flow through the capsule interior. Sufficient water to supply the oxygen needs of a near term embryo will be induced to flow at current speeds of just 0.2 knots. This passive flow comes at no metabolic cost to the embryo.

title: Electroreception in neonatal bonnethead sharks, Sphyrna tiburo

authors.affiliation: Hawaii Institute of Marine Biology, PO Box 1346, Kaneohe, HI, 96744, USA

abstract_text: Digital video analysis was used to quantify behavioural response of neonatal bonnethead sharks, Sphyrna tiburo, to prey-simulating electric fields. Sharks less than twelve hours post-parturition failed to demonstrate a positive feeding response to the electrodes, however, vigorous biting at the electrodes was observed in sharks greater than 24 hours post-parturition. Orientation behaviours were classified as one of four types: straight approach, single turn, looping return and spiral tracking where the shark appears to follow the voltage equipotential to the centre of the dipole. Most orientations to the dipole were from a distance of less than 10 cm with a maximum orientation distance of 22 cm. The mean threshold for initiation of orientation was 0.14 uV/cm with a minimum of less than 0.001 uV/cm. The mean value is almost double that obtained for juvenile scalloped hammerhead sharks, S. lewini, which require a mean stimulus of only 0.08 uV/cm to initiate an attack. The greater sensitivity of S. lewini may be attributed to their larger size and consequent longer ampullary canals.

title: Validation of otolith age estimates for the rainbow darter, Etheostoma caeruleum, in the James River of the southwest Missouri Ozarks

abstract_text: In the past 15 years there has been an emphasis on validation of age estimates for fish population studies. However, age estimates have been validated for few freshwater stream fish species; with a dearth of published age validation studies for North American darters of the genus Etheostoma. Traditionally darter ages have been obtained from scales or by length-frequency analysis, methods now known to be unreliable for many species. The purpose of this study was to evaluate otolith and scale age estimates for the rainbow darter, Etheostoma caeruleum, from the James River in the southwest Missouri Ozarks. Validity of age estimates was assessed by following the progression of annulus formation at the growing edge of scales and otoliths in fish captured throughout the year (edge analysis). Samples of 10-15 fish were taken by seine in each of 8 months from July 1996 through May 1997. Otoliths were viewed whole and in transverse section, and scales were viewed mounted between glass slides. Edge analysis of whole or sectioned otoliths indicated that one opaque annulus was formed per year in the otoliths, primarily during summer months. High agreement between sectioned and whole otolith ages (75% exact agreement, 99% within one year) indicates that consistent, valid ages can be obtained for Etheostoma caeruleum using either otolith method. Otolith age estimates ranged from 0-4 years. There was no clear pattern discerned in timing of scale annulus formation, and scale age estimates tended to be lower than otolith age estimates. Our results suggest that scale age estimates for darters should be made with caution.

title: Age, growth and reproduction of the gray triggerfish (Balistes capriscus) in the eastern Gulf of Mexico

abstract_text: Gray triggerfish (Balistes capriscus) commonly occur in the Gulf of Mexico recreational and commercial reef fish fisheries. Yet life history information needed for proper fisheries assessment of this species is inadequate. We sampled 679 gray triggerfish (103-725 mm FL) from the eastern Gulf of Mexico to assess their age structure, growth, mortality, and reproduction. Marginal-increment analysis and oxy-tetracycline injected fish failed to validate annual formation of rings in the dorsal spine; however, data from other studies indicates rings are formed once a year. Assuming rings are annual, ages ranged from 0 to 14 years. The von Bertalanffy growth parameters were Linf = 625 mm FL, k=0.152, and t0=-1.9 for combined sexes. The age of full recruitment was 4 years to the commercial fishery and 3 years to the recreational fishery. Estimates of total instantaneous mortality ranged from 0.742 to 0.836. The mean length of males was significantly larger than females, and the overall sex ratio was 2.1:1 in favor of males. No immature males were observed in our samples. Most females were mature by age 1 (87.5%) and 250 mm FL (91%). Ovaries containing vitellogenic oocytes were observed from June to September indicating that gray triggerfish spawn during the summer. Total fecundities ranged from 213,912 to 1,172,854 oocytes from females ranging 194 to 489 mm FL.

abstract_text: Florida's Fisheries-Independent Monitoring (FIM) program began collecting sheepshead, for life-history analyses, throughout the nearshore waters of Florida in 1993. More than 1,050 sheepshead (653 females, and 430 males), ranging in size from 107-522 mm FL, have been collected in the Tampa Bay estuary. Ages were estimated after the annuli were independently counted six times from thin-sectioned sagittae. Marginal increment analysis demonstrated that a single increment minimum occurred during May-June. Sheepshead reached a maximum age of 14 years. Analyses of the von Bertalanffy growth models showed that females and males grew at similar rates through age five, but that after age five the predicted lengths for females were greater than those for males. A previous Fisheries-Dependent (FD) study conducted in Louisiana waters indicated that sheepshead there grew faster and achieved older ages than did those from Tampa Bay. Although there may be subspecific (A. probatocephalus probatocephalus in Tampa Bay and A. probatocephalus oviceps in Louisiana) differences in age and growth, differences in sampling design (FIM vs. FD) most likely explain the disparity in growth model results.

title: Development of the lateral line system in the shovelnose sturgeon, Scaphirhynchus platorynchus

abstract_text: The shovelnose sturgeon, Scaphirhynchus platorynchus, normally develops over a 10 day period at 18 °C. During the first 45 hours post-fertilization, three preotic (anterodorsal, anteroventral and otic) and three postotic (medial, supratemporal and posterior) lateral line placodes arise within the cephalic ectoderm. Lateral line ganglia are formed in each placode from endogenous neuroblasts which migrate from the placodes at 60 hours post-fertilization. Placodes begin to elongate into sensory ridges a few hours before hatching, and by the time hatching occurs, at about 106 hours post-fertilization, neuromasts are erupting in the central zones of the otic and caudal anterodorsal sensory ridges. By four days post-hatch, an exposed mechanosensory lateral line extends from the dorsal zone of the anteroventral sensory ridge to the supra- and infra-orbital zones of the anterodorsal ridge. At 10 days post-hatch, the larva is feeding and has a mechanosensory lateral line that extends from the rostrum to the trunk and includes neuromasts from all six dorsolateral placodes. Electroreceptive ampullary organs, which arise from the anteroventral, anterodorsal, otic and supratemporal placodes begin to erupt just before the onset of feeding, and are fully developed by the time canals begin to form around the neuromast lines at twelve days post-hatch.

abstract_text: One possible cause implicated in worldwide amphibian declines is increased ultraviolet-B radiation (UV-B) brought on by anthropogenic thinning of the ozone layer. Due to the ozone hole, increased UV-B is most pronounced over Antarctica in winter, but ozone-poor air drifts northward over the southern cone of South America in early spring when frogs there begin to breed, thus potentially exposing their eggs and larvae to damaging amounts of UV-B. Damage from UV-B at that time is expected to be intense, especially since UV-B levels there prior to the first appearance of the ozone hole were not high. We report preliminary results from a multi-year study of potential UV-B effects on survival, growth, malformations, and DNA damage of developing eggs and larvae of Pleurodema bufonina in southern Argentina. In none of four populations studied so far have we found evidence of a negative effect of ambient UV-B.

title: Variability in exposure of amphibian embryos to UV-B radiation

authors.affiliation: USGS Midcontinent Ecological Science Center, Aldo Leopold Wilderness Research Institute, PO Box 8089, Missoula, MT 59807 USA

abstract_text: In the last 20 years, thinning stratospheric ozone has resulted in a 5-10% increase in UV-B radiation at the Earth's surface, poleward above 40° latitude. Field experiments that have shown increased mortality of amphibian embryos exposed to ambient sunlight, compared to those exposed to sunlight with UV-B removed, have lead to a hypothesis that increased UV-B radiation has contributed to amphibian declines. However, measurements of incident UV-B are missing from most of these studies, and variability in UV-B has not been examined. There are several sources of variation in the UV-B radiation to which embryos may be exposed, including annual variation in UV-B, seasonal gradients in UV-B, annual variation in amphibian breeding phenology, and local geographic variation in breeding phenology. I used satellite-based estimates of UV-B radiation and observations of amphibian breeding phenology in northern Colorado to estimate the range of variation in UV-B. Erythemal exposure (UV-B weighted by the action spectrum for human skin irritation) increases by 80% from 1 May to 30 June, and breeding activity may vary by 30 days from year to year and 14 days across an elevation gradient. Mean 10-day erythemal exposure for two populations of boreal chorus frogs, Pseudacris maculata, ranged between 192 and 388, and the mean exposure between populations of P. maculata and boreal toads, Bufo boreas, on elevation gradients increased by 21 and 28%, respectively. The increase in UV-B radiation due to ozone thinning is small relative to variation in UV-B to which embryos may be exposed.

title: Nest-site choice in a turtle with temperature-dependent sex determination

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology & Genetics, Program in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, Iowa State University, Ames, IA 50011 USA

abstract_text: The role of nest-site choice in the population biology of species with temperature-dependent sex determination (TSD) is virtually unexplored despite its importance in theoretical models for the evolution of sex ratio in such species. In those models, the evolution of sex ratio is largely determined by heritable variation in maternal choice of thermal qualities of nest sites. This ongoing 3-year field study examined thermally-dependent nest-site choice in a marked population of painted turtles that has been the focus of long-term studies of TSD. Analyses to date indicate that individual turtles exhibit significant fidelity to nest sites with similar amounts of surrounding vegetation cover. In other words, some turtles consistently prefer unshaded sites and vice versa. Because vegetational cover is a reasonable predictor of nest thermal environments and offspring sex ratios in this population, these findings suggest that nest-site choice and, hence, TSD may be able to evolve in response to environmental change. abstract_text: For the last decade, interest in modeling chelonian growth has increased and provided a framework for better understanding of this life history trait. Modeling growth generates variables that can be used as life history descriptors, and in unified comparative studies. With a long list of models, the question becomes which one to use? To choose among models, we must first understand the basic assumptions of the typical linear, quadratic, allometric, Johnson, Putter, von Bertalanffy, Gompertz and Logistic algorithms: 1) age is known, 2) growth follows the specified algorithm, 3) seasonal effects are absent and 4) genetic effects are minimal. Assumption one is circumvented using mark/recapture analogues of the aforementioned models, while assumption two is eliminated by using robust models like the Richard's, Schnute, Baker and Francis. New insights into modeling have allowed us to include seasonality; however, our knowledge of genetic effects does not presently allow us to correct existing models. We will discuss and present the value of certain mark/recapture growth models, by fitting mock and actual data sets to the von Bertalanffy, Gompertz, Logistic, Richard's and Schnute mark/recapture analogues.

title: Maternal effects, nest-site choice, and the maintenance of temperature-dependent sex determination

abstract_text: The adaptive value, if any, of temperature-dependent sex determination (TSD) is uncertain in reptiles. Suggested mechanisms include differential fitness between offspring sexes, dependent on maternal condition. Thus, females with the ability to assess environmental conditions that produce the sex whose fitness benefits most from maternal condition would have a selective advantage. This presentation reports a three-year field study on nest-site choice in the painted turtle, Chrysemys picta, a species exhibiting TSD. No relationship was found between egg mass and nest-site choice for the three years of the study. Although egg mass may not influence nest-site choice in painted turtles, other maternal effects that remain unexplored may play a role in nest-site choice and the maintenance of TSD.

title: Hearing in elasmobranchs: a review

authors.affiliation: Rosenstiel School of Marine and Atmospheric Science, University of Miami, Miami Florida 33149, USA

abstract_text: A brief history is provided of the studies which established that elasmobranchs not only detect underwater sounds, but respond to them in ways that suggested a rapid ability to locate specific sound-sources. The latter included acoustical features that mimicked sounds produced by struggling prey as well as providing a point-source to observe the behavioral activities of such predators. The rapid speed in locating sound-sources by free-ranging sharks created controversy, however. An important theory, at the time, precluded fishes, and particularly sharks, from directional hearing in the acoustical far-field (distances beyond one wavelength of a sound). Repeated confirmation that sharks could accomplish such a feat during the late '60s - mid 70s resulted in several new theories that could account for rapid directional hearing by these animals. These theories will also be briefly reviewed as will be the findings that resulted from a renewed interest in the neural mechanisms of elasmobranch hearing in the '80s. title: Sensory biology of vision in the elasmobranchs

abstract_text: The visual system of elasmobranchs is reviewed with respect to structure, function and behavior. As a general review, the visual systems of elasmobranchs and teleosts are compared and contrasted. Similar visual structures and functions of phylogenetically unrelated elasmobranchs are shown to occur in species occupying similar habitats and often displaying comparable behaviors. For example, the vertical slit pupil is found in active, pelagic and epibenthic elasmobranchs as widely divergent as carcharhinid sharks and myliobatid rays. Likewise, a strong correlation is found between depth of occurrence and position of the peak spectral absorption of the visual pigment, regardless of systematic affiliation. Performance testing of the visual system also reveals features adaptive to behavior and environment. Since the majority of information on visual performance has been gleaned from the lemon shark (Negaprion brevirostris), that visual system is reviewed. Correlates between visual structure, function and behavior show that the lemon shark has an ecologically broad period of activity and is able to carry out its normal behavior throughout the entire diel period. The review ends with an unexpected finding relating the lemon shark's visual pigments to habitat changes with aging. The final conclusion is that an understanding of how elasmobranch visual structure and function are correlated with behavior and ecology is barely at a beginning stage, and the field of elasmobranch vision, even after extensive study in recent decades, remains wide open. title: The elasmobranch mechanosensory lateral line system: form and function?

abstract_text: The biological function of the mechanosensory lateral line in relation to ecology and behavior is essentially unknown in elasmobranch fishes. One function of the teleost lateral line is to facilitate prey detection, but does the elasmobranch mechanosensory system possess the morphology and organization to support a role in prey localization and capture? General organization of the ventral lateral line system was examined in several representative batoid species (Dasyatis sabina, Raja eglanteria, Narcine brasiliensis, Gymnura micrura) in relation to their food habits and feeding behavior. authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, University of Guelph, Guelph, Ontario, N1G 2W1

abstract_text: My research concerns the conservation of quantitative trait loci (QTL) coding for the quantitative trait of upper thermal tolerance (UTT) (resistance time in the zone of maximal thermal stress) in commercial rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) populations. Previous research indicates the existence of four major QTL for UTT segregating in inbred lines selected for response to this trait. Individuals used in this study are the result of intra- and interstrain cross progeny of two unselected strains of commercial rainbow trout. Parental fish were derived from the combination of two grandsires and 12 grandams within each strain. Preliminary analysis indicates that major allelic variants are segregating in these hatchery strains for the previously identified UTT QTL. The ongoing survey of this progeny generation may reveal additional QTL allelic variants. Later work will attempt to determine the physiological mechanism by which the marked quantitative trait loci contribute to the total phenotype by assessing linkage between candidate coding loci (e.g. heat-shock proteins [hsps]) and variation in neutral microsatellite markers. The discovery of QTL-associated variance for this trait in strains unselected for UTT suggests that QTL variants for upper temperature tolerance may be fairly widespread in natural populations of rainbow trout.

title: A microsatellite assessment of within-river population structuring associated with the number of spawning/nursery grounds in Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar)

authors.affiliation: CIRSA, Universite Laval, Pavillon Vachon, Departement de Biologie, Quebec G1K 7P4
CIRSA, Universite Laval, Pavillon Vachon, Departement de Biologie, Quebec G1K 7P4
CIRSA, Universite Laval, Pavillon Vachon, Departement de Biologie, Quebec G1K 7P4

abstract_text: It has been proposed that population structure of aquatic organisms is determined by the number of environmental settings allowing completion of their life cycles. In this study, we test the hypothesis that this leads to the development of within-river population structuring associated with the existing number of spawning/nursery areas in anadromous Atlantic salmon. A total of 700 alevins sampled shortly after emergence (50 fish x 7 sites x 2 years) were genotyped using five microsatellite loci. Heterogeneity in allele frequency distribution, translating into significant Fst values among all pairwise comparisons of sites were observed for the two consecutive years of sampling. These parameters were lower among inter-annual samples of a same site than among sites. The majority of samples also clustered by sites in a neighbor-joining tree built from chord-distance. These results therefore support the hypothesis that genetic population substructuring in Atlantic salmon may develop at a very small geographic scale, as a consequence of the existing number of grounds favoring survival of young life-history stages. Because salmon associated with such population subunits may develop local adaptations, conservation and management policies should be planned to preserve their genetic integrity.

title: Preliminary investigation of microsatellite loci in red snapper (Lutjanus campechanus) in the northern Gulf of Mexico

authors.affiliation: Department of Wildlife and Fisheries Sciences, Center for Biosystematics and Biodiversity, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX USA
Department of Wildlife and Fisheries Sciences, Center for Biosystematics and Biodiversity, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX USA

abstract_text: The red snapper (Lutjanus campechanus) is one of the most economically-important fishes in the Gulf of Mexico (Gulf). Previous analyses of mitochondrial (mt) DNA in the northern Gulf detected no significant differences in haplotype frequency across a geographic gradient and no partitioning of uncommon haplotypes, indicating that red snappers in the northern Gulf comprise a single genetic population. However, differences in mtDNA haplotype diversity among several samples indicated that some level of genetic population structure exists, and that perhaps a more rapidly-evolving genetic character might reveal that structure. We therefore developed a suite of highly polymorphic DNA microsatellite loci to further examine the partitioning of genetic variation in this species. A subgenomic library of restriction fragments was screened with di-, tri-, and tetra-nucleotide repeat and several microsatellite loci were identified and sequenced. Oligonucleotide primers for amplification of loci via polymerase chain reaction were developed. Polymorphism in microsatellite allele size was scored on denaturing polyacrylamide gels. Microsatellite allele frequencies from different year classes and different regions were compared to further test the hypothesis that red snapper from the northern Gulf comprise a single genetic population.

title: A review of the appendicular skeleton in amphisbaenians (Reptilia: Squamata)

authors.affiliation: George Washington University, Department of Biological Sciences, Washington, DC 20052 USA

abstract_text: While reduction and loss of external limbs are hallmarks of amphisbaenian evolution, internal girdle and hindlimb remnants in some amphisbaenian taxa have been known for many years. However, less than half of the known genera have been surveyed for internal remnants of the appendicular skeleton and these structures have not been systematically compared. I surveyed the appendicular skeleton in all extant genera of amphisbaenians via the preparation and study of radiographs, dry skeletons, and cleared and stained specimens and compared them to each other as well as to other non- and reduced-limbed squamates. This study revealed that relative reduction of girdle and limb elements is diverse among the group. Variability in bony and cartilagenous components of the girdle and limb remnants appears to contain useful information for ongoing phylogenetic studies of amphisbaenian interrelationships. All amphisbaenians retain at least one bony pelvic element but many amphisbaenians have completely lost the pectoral girdle. Among squamates, regardless of the degree of limb reduction or loss, the pelvic girdle never completely disappears in amphisbaenians or 'lizards' as it does in most snakes, and the pectoral girdle never completely disappears in 'lizards' as it does in many amphisbaenians and all snakes.

title: The phylogeny and evolution of viviparity in the alticolor and elongatus lineages of Liolaemus lizards

authors.affiliation: Ecology, Evolution & Conservation Biology, MS 314, University of Nevada, Reno, Reno, NV 89557, USA

abstract_text: The genus Liolaemus (Iguania: Tropiduridae) is the largest genus of lizards in the Southern Hemisphere. Partially as a consequence of this diversity, the intrageneric relationships within Liolaemus are largely enigmatic. Approximately half of the nearly 170 described taxa in the genus belong to the chiliensis group. Within this large clade, several species groups have been informally recognized including the alticolor and the elongatus groups. I undertook an analysis of mitochondrial DNA to ascertain the relationships among members of the alticolor and elongatus species groups to (1) determine if members of each of these species groups formed monophyletic lineages; and (2) address the evolution of viviparity within these groups. I sequenced about 700 bp (167 informative) of the mitochondrial 12S gene for nearly all described and several undescribed species within the two species groups. A maximum parsimony analysis recovered three equally parsimonious trees. A consensus tree of the mtDNA results were then combined with additional evidence derived from morphological and ecological studies. The combined phylogenetic hypothesis suggests that the two groups are indeed monophyletic. Furthermore, viviparity appears to have evolved independently several times within the alticolor group, but only once for the elongatus group, wherein, one species may have reverted to oviparous reproduction.

title: Genetic variation in Rana sphenocephala in response to an agricultural chemical: implications for amphibian conservation

authors.affiliation: 105 Tucker Hall, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO 65211-7400, USA

abstract_text: The amount of genetic variability present may indicate a species' ability to adapt to a stressful environment and can be examined in a quantitative genetic analysis. Currently, numerous conservation efforts are being devoted to determining whether amphibian species are in decline, as many studies would suggest. Therefore, because amphibians are amenable to quantitative genetic analyses and because their numbers may be declining due to changes in their environment, these organisms serve as an excellent model for examining the relationship between the amount of genetic variability present in populations and adaptability in changing environments. Using tadpoles of a single southern leopard frog (Rana sphenocephala) population, I examined the amount of genetic variability among full- and half-sib families with respect to their sensitivity to both lethal (time-to-death) and sublethal (changes in activity) levels of the agricultural chemical, carbaryl. Analyses of both time-to-death and activity data indicate significant differences among full sib families, suggesting a great deal of variability, genetic or environmental, present in the responses to this environmental stressor. There were also significant differences among half sib families in the degree to which activity was reduced by sublethal carbaryl levels, indicating that this variability has a genetic basis.

title: Conservation genetics of the Mojave fringe-toed lizard, Uma scoparia, in California

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, University of Toronto and Centre for Biodiversity and Conservation Biology, Royal Ontario Museum, 100 Queen's Park, Toronto, Ontario, M5S 2C6

abstract_text: The Mojave fringe-toed lizard, Uma scoparia, is restricted to sand dunes in the Mojave Desert, existing in 25 known localities. Because of this species' restriction to sand dunes, it has been considered a species of special concern. Many populations are on the decline due to habitat destruction, misuse of off-road vehicles and possibly a significant increase in raven numbers. The determination of the extent and geographic distribution of genetic diversity among the Mojave fringe-toed lizards is imperative for conservation and potential augmentation of endangered populations. Augmentation of the Fort Irwin population is essential due to the rapidly declining population size, which is critical since small populations are highly susceptible to stochastic events. If this population is to remain reproductively viable, then genetic viability and integrity, including local adaptations must be maintained by introducing 'sister' populations; individuals from populations that are most similar genetically. The mitochondrial genes ATPase 6 and cytochrome b were sequenced for 27 U. scoparia from 8 localities, using U. notata as outgroup. In total, 1676 combined base pairs were sequenced, of which 170 were potentially phylogenetically informative. Results of parsimony analysis revealed that the most closely related populations to NTC Fort Irwin are the dunes at Kelso and Pisgah Crater, located southeast of the base.

title: Toward the phylogeny of the family Lacertidae: implications from mitochondrial DNA 12S, 16S and COI gene sequences (Reptilia: Squamata)

authors.affiliation: Centre for Biodiversity and Conservation Biology, Royal Ontario Museum, 100 Queen's Park, Toronto, Ontario, Canada M5S 2C6

abstract_text: A phylogeny of the family Lacertidae was derived from mtDNA gene sequence data. Thirty-two species, representing 22 currently recognized genera and subgenera, were included in the analysis. A total of 3,600 base pairs was obtained and aligned from 12S, 16S and COI gene sequences. A preferred tree was selected based on weighted parsimony and functional ingroup and outgroup analyses. Decay analysis, bootstrap and permutation tail probability were used to evaluate support for the recovered nodes. The genus Gallotia was resolved as the basal taxon and the sister group of all remaining lacertids. Takydromus branched off next. All African lacertids grouped together, and formed a monophyletic clade with the Eurasian genera Eremias and Ophisops. The remaining Eurasian lacertids sequentially branched off near the base of the tree in a 'comb-like' fashion. The basal position of Gallotia and the monophyly of African lacertids are consistent with previous hypotheses. The European-origin hypothesis of lacertids is favored, and the distribution of lacertids in Africa is likely a dispersal event.

title: Snake vertebrae do the twist

authors.affiliation: Dept. Biology, Univ. Michigan, Ann Arbor MI 48109, USA

abstract_text: The zygosphene-zygantrum articulations of snake vertebrae are hypothesized to restrict or eliminate vertebral torsion. This hypothesis is apparently based solely on the inference of function from structure, despite contradictory evidence. Gasc (1974, Mem. Mus. Nat. Hist. Nat., Paris Ser. A Zool. 83:1-182) measured vertebral torsion of 1-2°/joint in dried Python skeletons, but his results are seldom cited. I observed axial torsion during lateral undulation and feeding in Pituophis melanoleucus. To determine whether apparent axial torsion results from differential movement of the left and right body walls, combined lateral and vertical bending, or actual torsion at the vertebral joints, I examined close-up video images of crawling P. melanoleucus and digitized macro video images of torsion in fresh sections of the trunk. To measure vertebral torsion, I clamped sections of 10 vertebrae at one end and twisted the free end by hand; the limits of twisting were clearly detectable and were reached before the movement produced any axial bending. Freely crawling P. melanoleucus exhibited negligible lifting, moderate differential movement of the left and right body walls, and apparent torsion of 0.02-2.4°/vertebra. Fresh trunk sections allowed actual torsion of 0.3-1.1°/vertebra, which produced substantial overall torsion when added over several vertebrae. Therefore, the observed torsion was likely produced by differential movement of the left and right body walls combined with real torsion at the vertebral joints. Despite the mechanical restrictions imposed by the complex articulations, vertebral torsion occurs in snakes and appears to be functionally important in many kinds of snake movements.

title: Effects of an acetylcholinesterase insecticide on amphibian communities under different levels of biotic stress

authors.affiliation: 212 Tucker Hall, Dept. of Biology, University of Missouri-Columbia, Columbia, MO 65211 USA

abstract_text: Widespread use of agricultural chemicals makes it increasingly likely that non-target wildlife could be exposed to contamination. Many amphibian species utilize breeding habitats nested within or around agricultural areas, therefore population and community dynamics may be influenced or altered by exposure to chemicals. The chemical used in this experiment, carbaryl, is the active ingredient in the insecticide Sevin. This chemical acts through acetylcholinesterase inhibition, and is known to affect amphibian activity and behavior. The objectives of this experiment were to determine differential susceptibility to carbaryl among species, the effect of the chemical under different biotic conditions, and the indirect effects of the chemical. To do this, I used three species of anurans in outdoor cattle tanks: Hyla versicolor (gray treefrog), Bufo woodhousii (toad) and Rana clamitans (green frog). Twelve experimental treatments were manipulated for density (high or low), predator (presence or absence of Notophthalmus viridescens) and chemical level (0, 3.5, or 7.0 mg/l of carbaryl). Results showed that the chemical significantly affected size at metamorphosis in H. versicolor. A predator by chemical effect in H. versicolor was significant; in the presence of the predator, tadpoles at high chemical levels had a larger size at metamorphosis than other classes. Chemical effects on survival at metamorphosis were significant in B. woodhousii and H. versicolor; higher chemical levels significantly reduced survival. The chemical interacts with biotic factors in ways that would not be predictable from two-factor experiments. Chemical by density interactions were significant in B. woodhousii and H. versicolor. This experiment does indicate differential susceptibility among species and noted that differences in biotic conditions affect the potency of the chemical.

title: Biogeographic area relationships of lowland neotropical rainforests based on cladistic analysis of anurans and lizards

authors.affiliation: Division of Herpetology, Natural History Museum and Biodiversity Research Center, and Department of Systematics and Ecology, The University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS 66045, USA

abstract_text: In order to determine biogeographic relationships, Parsimony Analysis of Endemicity (PAE) was applied to presence/absence of species of anurans in 14 localities of lowland Neotropical rainforests in the Chocoan Region, Central America, Amazon Basin, and Brazilian Atlantic Forest. Phylogenetic Analysis Using Parsimony (PAUP 3.1) of 340 species led to two most parsimonious area cladograms (TL = 475, CI = 0.705). The strict consensus showed a basal polytomy among three regions: (1) Central America and Choco, (2) Amazon Basin, and (3) Atlantic Forest. Within the Amazon Basin, the localities in the Upper Amazonian in Peru and Ecuador were separated from those in the Lower Amazon Basin (Guianan Region + Belem). A PAE of presence/absence of 108 lizard species in 13 areas in Central America and the Amazon Basin led to a single most parsimonious area cladogram (TL = 156, CI = 0.692). The Central American localities were separated from those of the Amazon Basin. Within the Amazon Basin, a separation between Upper Amazonian in Ecuador and Peru and Lower Amazonian was observed. This pattern is similar to the pattern obtained from the anuran PAE.

title: Interactions among parental and hybrid leopard frog larvae in experimental ponds: implications for the coexistence of genotypes

authors.affiliation: Division of Biological Sciences, University of Missouri, Columbia, MO 65211-7400, USA

abstract_text: A major focus for contemporary studies of natural hybridization is experimental determination of the relative fitness of parental and hybrid genotypes and measurements of the interactions between the genotype and environment. Natural hybridization occurs between two anuran species, Rana blairi and Rana sphenocephala. To determine the relative fitness of parental and hybrid genotypes in sympatric leopard frog populations in Missouri, I examined the performance of parental and hybrid larvae to measure differences in viability. Artificial crosses between R. blairi and R. sphenocephala produced two parental and three hybrid genotypes. Resultant larvae were reared in experimental ponds in single- and mixed-genotype populations. Analyses of variance indicated that R. sphenocephala decreased its larval period length when reared with F1 backcross hybrid larvae relative to when reared alone. F1 backcross hybrid ponds produced more metamorphs when larvae were reared with either parental species relative to when reared alone. When reared together, both R. sphenocephala and F1 hybrids metamorphosed at larger body masses than when reared separately. These results indicate that parental and hybrid genotypes perform at equivalent or higher levels when reared together compared to single-genotype ponds. Such evidence suggests that larval dynamics may play an important role in maintaining the coexistence of genotypes in this hybrid zone.

title: The Rana livida complex: systematics of a group of Vietnamese waterfall frogs

authors.affiliation: Centre for Biodiversity and Conservation Biology, Royal Ontario Museum, & Department of Zoology, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON M5S 2C6

abstract_text: Remarkable morphological similarity among the cascade (waterfall) ranids of southeast Asia has made them a taxonomic bane for 160 years. Central among this confusion has been the green cascade frog, Rana livida. Inhabiting the fast moving mountain rivers and forests of Indochina, this stink frog has long been suspected of being composed of several species. Recently collected specimens from Vietnam keyed out to R. livida, but exhibited evident morphological differences across populations. A combination of morphology, morphometrics, DNA content analysis, and allozyme electrophoresis was used to investigate whether or not any of these morphotypes were distinct species. The results from this investigation suggested the presence of 5 distinct species. A phylogeny for the group using partial mitochondrial 16S gene sequences was estimated. A 537 base pair region yielded 91 potentially informative characters. Maximum parsimony was used to evaluate the data. Because these species were identified over a very small portion of the geographic range of the Rana livida group, it is expected that this phylogeny will be expanded as more species of this poorly understood complex are discovered.

title: Aspects of the physiological ecology of the desert horned lizard, Phrynosoma platyrhinos

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, University of California, Los Angeles, CA 90095 USA

abstract_text: Deserts are characterized by extreme environmental and resource variation; many desert reptiles have the ability to tolerate these stresses through behavioral and physiological mechanisms. Desert horned lizards, Phrynosoma platyrhinos, are one of the most common lizards in the Mojave desert. Horned lizards are morphologically adapted to exploit ants as their primary food source, and they are characterized by certain aspects of typical sit-and-wait predators. It has been suggested that desert horned lizards should have relatively low energy requirements because of their foraging strategy and because they inhabit an area typified by low resource availability. To address this hypothesis, I used doubly labeled water to measure the energy and water turnover of a population of desert horned lizards over a five year study period. The annual rainfall of the study area varied during the study period such that there were normal, very wet and very dry conditions. This allowed me to examine the physiological plasticity of horned lizards. The results of my research will be presented.

title: A comparison of ontogenetic and geographic variation of the Amazonian tree frog Hyla geographica

authors.affiliation: Department of Biology, UNC Wilmington, Wilmington, N.C. 28405

abstract_text: This study contributes to the knowledge of Amazonian herpetology by evaluating the mensurable and meristic characters associated with ontogeny, sexual dimorphism, and geographic variation of the Amazonian tree frog Hyla geographica. The taxonomic significance of the displayed variations was analyzed by evaluating external characters. Four hundred eleven specimens from the following museums were examined: Museum of Comparative Zoology at Harvard, U.S. National Museum of Natural History, and Chicago Museum of Natural History. This analysis included population samples from the following political entities: Trinidad, Colombia, French Guiana, Guyana, Suriname, Ecuador, Bolivia, Peru, and Brazil. Mensurable characters obtained were: head-length (HL), head-width (HW), tympanum-diameter (TD), femur-length (FL), and snout-vent-length (SVL). These measurements were used to calculate morphology ratios for analysis of ontogenetic growth variations. The means, standard deviation, and range of all mensurable characters and growth ratios were determined. Distribution patterns of pigments were coded and recorded for all specimens. The pigment patterns, or absence of pigments were recorded for the snout, venter, dorsum, thigh, flank, upper arm, and dorsal aspect of the head. All specimens were examined for sexual maturity. The variations of the mensurable characters, morphological ratios, and patterns of pigment distribution suggest that the populations of H. geographica do not display significant geoclines and, therefore, are one widely distributed species.

title: Cytochrome b based gene genealogy of the common garter snake, Thamnophis sirtalis

authors.affiliation: Department of Zoology, University of Guelph, Guelph, Ontario CANADA N1G 2W1
California Academy of Sciences, San Francisco, California 94118-4599 USA

abstract_text: Thamnophis sirtalis is a widely distributed, highly variable, snake which is common throughout much of its North American range. Historically, this species has been subdivided into many subspecies based predominantly on geographical variation in colour pattern, although there is also variation in life history traits and meristic characters. Of the twelve currently recognized subspecies, several meet in broad areas of intergradation which are forms of hybrid zones where there is introgression between distinct gene pools. In order to infer the evolutionary relationship of snakes on either side of these hybrid zones, a mitochondrial DNA gene genealogy was constructed. Cytochrome b was amplified from over 123 snakes representing most of the entire range. A 385 or 780 bp portion was sequenced on a ABI automated sequencer at the GenAlyTic facility at the University of Guelph and yielded 45 distinct haplotypes with 73 phylogenetically informative characters. The heuristic search option of Paup was used to find all equally most parsimonious trees (320 trees, length 126 steps, CI=0.71, RI=0.92, RC=0.65). The resulting strict consensus tree revealed three distinct clades whose geographical distributions are not concordant with those of currently recognized subspecies.

title: Influence of hydrographic structure upon genetic structure in brook charr (Salvelinus fontinalis) populations in national parks of eastern Canada

authors.affiliation: GIROQ, Departement de Biologie, Universite Laval, Quebec, Canada G1K 7P4
GIROQ, Departement de Biologie, Universite Laval, Quebec, Canada G1K 7P4

abstract_text: Despite the abundance of studies of genetic diversity in freshwater fishes, few of them specifically addressed the role of habitat structure in partitioning genetic variance within and among populations. Microsatellite loci have recently been developed for Salvelinus fontinalis (Angers et al., 1995) and successfully used to assess population structure within the species. In this study, we analyzed the variability of six microsatellite loci among 25 brook charr populations samples (n=30) in order to correlate hydrographic structure with genetic organization. These populations originate from three Canadian National parks (Kouchibouguac, Fundy and Forillon), showing contrasting hydrographic structure. Considering the general characteristics of these habitats, we formulated the hypothesis that the ratio of interpopulation/intrapopulation genetic diversity will be inversely correlated with the potential for gene flow imposed by those systems. Results obtained supported our working hypotheses. Thus, the hierarchical analysis of molecular variance revealed that the lower ratio of interpopulation/intrapopulation genetic diversity was found in Kouchibouguac (high migration potential) [0.0703, P=0.01210] whereas an intermediate value was observed in Fundy (intermediate migration potential) [0.1771, P=0.00000]. The highest ratio was observed in Forillon (low migration potential) [1.6885, P=0.00000]. We discuss the importance of habitat complexity on genetic structure in the context of management and conservation.

title: Genetic diversity of the La Mauricie National Park brook charr (Salvelinus fontinalis)

authors.affiliation: Departement de biologie, Universite Laval, Sainte-Foy QC G1K 7P4
Departement de chimie-biologie, Universite du Quebec a Trois-Rivieres QC
Departement de chimie-biologie, Universite du Quebec a Trois-Rivieres QC

abstract_text: The identification of brook charr conservation units and processes responsible for their evolution are prerequisites to the conservation and management of the species in national parks. In this study we documented genetic diversity among brook charr populations from la Mauricie national park and investigated factors that can account for the variation observed. Thirty-six populations (n=30) from eight different drainages were genetically characterized at five microsatellites and mtDNA. The mtDNA homogeneity indicated a common refugial origin of all populations. In contrast, extensive polymorphism was observed at microsatellites. Eleven evolutionary lineages were identified and their divergence apparently predated the postglacial recolonization of the park, suggesting that the park was recolonized by multiple population waves from a single yet fragmented glacial refuge. Multivariate statistical analysis highlighted the role of hydrographic systems, altitude, and stocking as the main explanatory factors for the observed genetic structure. Altogether, these results suggest that the use of microsatellites may reorient our views about problems of temporal and geographical scales considered in conservation genetics.

title: Slowly-evolving proteins and higher-level snake phylogeny: a reanalysis

authors.affiliation: Biology Department, Rochester Institute of Technology, Rochester, NY 14623-9932 USA
George Washington University, Department of Biological Sciences, Washington, DC 20052 USA
Department of Vertebrate Zoology, National Museum of Natural History, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, DC 20056 USA

abstract_text: We reanalyzed the data of a recently published study of higher-level snake relationships, which was based on a UPGMA analysis of alleles at four "slowly-evolving" protein-coding loci. The distance matrix derived from these data contains a large number of ties, which are not explicitly revealed in many UPGMA programs. Our analyses of these data reveal that the single, well-resolved phenogram presented in the published study is only one among at least 9,999 equivalent UPGMA phenograms supported by the data, the consensus of which is largely unresolved. Additive distance analysis and character-based parsimony analysis of the same data yield even less resolution. Thus, regardless of one's preference regarding analytical approaches, the data in question are highly ambiguous concerning higher-level snake phylogeny. The highly resolved tree presented in the published study is an analytical artifact that was obtained only because the analysis failed to consider equivalent trees resulting from ties in the distance matrix.

title: Microsatellite variation in wild populations of lake trout (Salvelinus namaycush) from Lake Superior

Department of Biological Sciences, University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, Milwaukee, WI USA
Great Lakes Science Center, USGS, Ann Arbor, MI USA
Great Lakes Field Station, USGS, Ashland, WI USA

abstract_text: Microsatellite variation was surveyed in six populations of lean lake trout and two populations of siscowet lake trout from Lake Superior using heterologous primer pairs developed for brook trout (Salvelinus fontinalis) and Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar). The number of alleles varied from 4 to 21 at different loci. Mendelian inheritance was confirmed for all loci. title: Stock identification of dolphin, Coryphaena hippurus, in the western central Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico and eastern Caribbean using molecular genetic techniques

authors.affiliation: University of Charleston, Grice Marine Lab, 205 R. Johnson Rd., Charleston, SC 29412

abstract_text: The dolphin, Coryphaena hippurus, is a fast swimming, migratory, pelagic fish that supports important commercial and recreational fisheries throughout the tropical and subtropical waters of the world. Oxenford and Hunte (1986) suggested two distinct stocks exist in the western central Atlantic. The southern stock migrates from Grenada northwards to the Virgin Islands and then returns southeastwards in the Atlantic. The northern stock migrates from Puerto Rico northwards to North Carolina and returns via Bermuda. The purpose of my study is to test Oxenford and Hunte's (1986) two stock hypothesis and investigate the possible presence of additional stocks using mitochondrial DNA analysis. Dolphin samples were obtained throughout their range in the western central Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico, and Caribbean by port sampling and attending offshore fishing tournaments. Preliminary results from restriction fragment length polymorphisms of the ND-1 region of the mitochondrial genome will be reviewed. Significant genetic differences between geographic localities provides strong evidence of demographic isolation and indicates the need for independent management of individual stocks (Dixon 1992, Moritz 1994). In August 1997, the South Atlantic Fishery Management Council proposed management options for the highly migratory dolphin fishery. Data provided by this study on the stock identification of the dolphin should be beneficial to the management of this fishery throughout the western Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico, and Caribbean.

title: The structure of basking shark Cetorhinus maximus populations in the North-East Atlantic: development of genetic markers

abstract_text: Basking shark populations have been subject to exploitation for many years and are currently considered to be endangered in European waters. However, little is known of their population structure. In the recent past, population structure assessments have been made on the basis of capture-mark-recapture studies or differentiation of meristic and morphological characteristics of different stocks. However, for a species such as the basking shark, which are not easy to tag in large numbers, and which little is known about their ecology, a new approach is required. Molecular genetic methods are increasingly being used with success in determining the stock structure of commercially important fish species in both marine and freshwater environments. In particular, the use of microsatellite DNA sequences is finding increasing use in fisheries stock assessment. title: Fundulus diaphanus is the maternal parent of the clonal hybrid minnow Fundulus heteroclitus x Fundulus diaphanus

abstract_text: Fundulus heteroclitus is an abundant estuarine fish found along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of the United States. This species has been the subject of numerous investigations of its own biology and has been used as a tool to study xenobiotic metabolism, development, and ecology. Hybrids between Fundulus heteroclitus and F. diaphanus from Nova Scotia reproduce clonally, and thus all individuals are genetically identical. Heterozygosity at codominantly expressed enzyme loci is detectable for all enzymes for which the parental species differ, with the exception of isocitrate dehydrogenase for which the F. diaphanus is not expressed. abstract_text: RAPD markers are powerful tools in the analysis of genetic relationships and genetic diversity. abstract_text: Amphibians have been widely used as model systems for studying the early embryonic development of vertebrates. Although much of the early development of all amphibians is very similar, frogs and salamanders differ strikingly in the way they determine the germ cell lineage (the cells that will form eggs and sperm). The pattern observed in frogs is quite different than the one seen in other vertebrates; the salamander mechanism is apparently much more similar to that of birds and mammals. Although the pattern of germ cell formation has been elucidated in a wide variety of species, little is known about the genes governing this process. Because most major embryological events are controlled by genes that have been highly conserved evolutionarily, it is logical to conclude that genes involved in germ cell determination will also be similar in a wide variety of species. Three genes - daz, oct-3/4 and vasa - have been shown to be critical for germ cell determination in mammals. We have used phylogenetic methods to analyze the homologous genes from frogs and salamanders to investigate whether the evolution of germ cell specific genes reflects the mode of germ cell determination (salamanders being more similar to mammals) or the phylogenetic relationships of the organisms (salamanders and frogs being more closely related). Our preliminary results suggest that germ cell determining genes from two different salamanders are more closely related to the mammalian homologues than to anuran ones, supporting the idea that the evolution of the genes tracks the mode of cell determination rather than the animal phylogeny.
